h1: Building a modular identity system for your brewery's beers
title: Modular identity systems for breweries | Craft Beer School
desc: How a family identity system makes each new beer label faster to design, cheaper to produce and simpler to put through excise approval in India.
teaser: Eighteen labels in year one, each designed from scratch? There is a cheaper way that also looks better in the fridge.
standfirst: A growing range of beers needs a family look, not a pile of one-off labels. Here is what to fix, what to change per beer and how the system saves time and money on every new label.
sections: A logo alone will not carry eighteen labels

Count the labels you will need in your first year. A brewpub with 6 core beers and one seasonal a month needs 18 designs by December, more if each beer comes in 330 ml and 500 ml cans as well as 650 ml bottles. Designing each from scratch is slow and costly. It also leaves the fridge looking like 18 different breweries.

The answer is a modular identity system: a family of visual parts that work together wherever the brand appears. The parts are a main logo, alternate versions of it, a set of icons, textures, typefaces and a fixed colour palette. Used well, each new label feels fresh and the range still reads as one brewery. This guide, part of our series on branding a new brewery, splits those parts into what stays fixed and what changes per beer.
Fix the five things that make you recognisable

The fixed half is what a drinker spots from across the bar before reading a word. We would lock five things:

  • The main logo and where it sits. Same corner and same size on every can and bottle.
  • The typefaces. One for the beer name, one for everything else.
  • The layout grid. Beer name, style and ABV in the same places every time.
  • The brand colours. Two or three that appear on everything, kept apart from the beer colours.
  • The information panel. One template for the mandatory text, covered below.

If a new beer seems to need one of these five changed, it probably belongs to a separate range. That is a decision for the founders, not for the designer on a deadline.
Let colour and an icon tell one beer from the next

The changing half should stay small. For most ranges it is three things: the beer name, one accent colour and an illustration or icon. Icons and patterns do this job well because they read at a glance from across a bar. A witbier might get a pale orange with a coriander seed icon, a stout a near black with a cream accent.

Choose a palette of 12 accent colours on day one, so the designer picks rather than invents. Twelve covers a core range plus seasonals before anything repeats. It also stops two beers ending up in near-identical greens on the same shelf.

Every beer label in India carries mandatory text, from FSSAI labelling to whatever your state excise department asks for. The exact list varies by state and changes, so check the current notification or ask a licensing consultant. What the system adds is a fixed panel: one tested layout for that text, drawn for each pack you use.

Build it in three versions, for the 330 ml can, the 500 ml can and the 650 ml bottle. Once a panel has been accepted, a new beer changes only the fields that differ, such as name, style and ABV. The consultant and the excise office see a familiar layout each time, which makes every submission easier to check. Your designer also stops re-measuring type sizes on every new label.
The system pays for itself on volume

A system costs more at the start, because the designer has to think through future labels as well as the first. It pays back with every beer after that. Suppose a label from a blank page takes 5 working days and a label inside the system takes 1. At 18 labels a year that is 90 days of design against 18. Put your own designer's day rate against the 72 days saved and the sum makes itself.

Secondary marks earn their keep off the pack too. Plenty of people will not wear a T-shirt with a large logo across the chest, yet will happily wear a small icon from the system. The same icon works on coasters, the tap list and Instagram highlights.
Ask for files, not just a look

A system only works if you own the parts. Make sure the job hands over these:

  • The main logo as vector files, which scale from a coaster to a hoarding without losing detail.
  • Secondary builds: a horizontal version, a vertical version, a small icon and the tagline lock-up.
  • The colour palette in 4 formats: Pantone, CMYK, RGB and Hex.
  • Typography with usage rules and the font licences in your name.

Add two of our own for Indian packs: the panel templates above and the die-lines from your label supplier. Our guides on beer label design and can design cover the front of the pack. Deciding what to lock is harder than it looks from inside the brewery, which is why an outside eye with advertising experience helps.

Your first step this week: line up every label you have or sketch the planned range. Circle what is the same on all of them. Whatever is not circled is what your system has to fix.
Ankur Napa is a Master Brewer who also works in data and AI. Chatty Girija spent more than 30 years in advertising, hosts the Cheers Chatty Beer Podcast and teaches at Craft Beer School.
faqs: What is a modular identity system?
A set of visual parts, such as the main logo, alternate builds, icons, colours and typefaces, that work together so each new beer looks different but still belongs to your brewery.
What should stay the same on every beer label?
The logo and its position, the typefaces, the layout grid, the brand colours and the mandatory information panel.
Does a modular system help with excise label approval in India?
It helps on the design side, because a fixed panel layout means each new label changes only a few fields. Approval itself still follows your state's rules, which vary and change.
Is a system worth it for a small brewpub?
If you plan more than a handful of beers a year, usually yes. Each new label becomes a small job instead of a fresh design.
